analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from finalizing the Clean Water Act rule defining which waters are protected.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had one Republican sponsor and 38 Republican cosponsors, never left the Senate environment committee and received no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2014 the EPA and Army Corps of Engineers proposed a rule saying which streams, wetlands, and ponds count as 'waters of the United States' under the Clean Water Act. This bill would have prohibited the agencies from finalizing that rule, and from using it — or any rule or guidance substantially similar to it — in any decision about the scope or enforcement of the Clean Water Act. It even made using such a basis legal grounds for voiding any resulting rule or enforcement action. The bill sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners, farmers, homebuilders, real estate developers, and energy and mining companies that would face federal permitting requirements if more streams and wetlands were brought under Clean Water Act jurisdiction. Blocking the rule and any similar future effort would spare them those compliance costs.

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits the Army Secretary and EPA Administrator from finalizing the proposed 'Waters of the United States' rule, keeping the agencies from expanding which waters require federal permits. [S2]

It goes further than just killing the one rule: it bars the agencies from using that proposal or any 'substantially similar' rule or guidance as the basis for any Clean Water Act rulemaking or enforcement decision. [S3]
It makes using such a rule or guidance grounds for a court to vacate any resulting final rule, decision, or enforcement action, giving regulated parties a ready defense. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: If the bill had passed, the public would bear the cost in reduced protection for streams and wetlands that feed drinking water supplies and filter pollution, and communities downstream of discharges would have less federal recourse. Because the bill also blocked 'substantially similar' future rules, it would have locked in that narrower protection indefinitely.

drawbacks.text: Blocking the rule would have left the reach of the Clean Water Act uncertain after Supreme Court decisions limited federal jurisdiction over isolated waters and wetlands, leaving many waterways with unclear protection. [S2]

The bill did not just reject one proposal — it barred any 'substantially similar' rule or guidance and allowed vacating enforcement actions, an unusually broad restriction on the agencies' ability to interpret the law at all. [S3]

An honest supporter would acknowledge the tradeoff: farmers and landowners feared federal permitting requirements over ditches, ponds, and dry streambeds on their property, but narrowing jurisdiction shifts pollution risk downstream to the public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered a clear compliance benefit to landowners and regulated industries while leaving the scope of the nation's water pollution law unsettled and cutting protection for smaller streams and wetlands that feed drinking water. The public cost ran in the opposite direction from the concentrated benefit, and the bill's bar on any similar future rule went well beyond rejecting a single proposal.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Barrasso introduced the bill on June 19, 2014, with 30 original Senate cosponsors, all Republicans. [S3]
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, which was its only committee referral. [S1]
The committee took no further action; the full action history shows no hearings, markups, or floor votes after referral. [S5]
The bill ended with 38 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support, and never received a vote in either chamber before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Regulated industries — agriculture, developers, and energy and mining firms — were better off because the bill died only in the sense that the underlying outcome they wanted (no expanded Clean Water Act rule) largely held anyway through the end of the Congress, while the public retained the existing (if contested) scope of federal water protection. No one gained the bill's sweeping statutory bar.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulated industries; rule's fate stayed with courts

for.name: Sen. John Barrasso
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 38 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the Senate Minority Leader and other party leaders.

against.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 cosponsors were Republicans and there were no Democratic cosponsors; the Democratic chair of the referral committee never took it up.

industries.note: The proposed rule would have extended federal permitting to more streams, ditches, and wetlands on farmland, and this bill would have blocked that. Farmers' compliance savings would come at the cost of weaker pollution controls on waterways the public uses.
Developers face Clean Water Act permitting when building on or near wetlands; the bill would have removed the expansion of those requirements and given a defense against enforcement.

Broader water jurisdiction means more discharge permits and enforcement exposure for extraction and pipeline projects; the bill would have barred the agencies from using the expanded definition in any enforcement decision.

industries.industry: Water utilities and public water suppliers
industries.note: Rules protecting upstream streams and wetlands reduce treatment costs and protect source water for utilities serving the public, though some utilities also opposed certain rule provisions on permitting grounds.
